questions.questionText: Consider that the quick sort algorithm is used to sort an array of $n$ distinct randomly ordered elements. In every call, the pivot is chosen as the first element of the current subarray. Let $T(n)$ denote the expected time to sort the array. Assume that the time to partition is linear in the size of the current subarray. Which of the following recurrence relations correctly represents $T(n)$ in this scenario? $T(n)=T(1)+T(n-1)+O(n)$ $T(n)=T\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+T\left(\frac{3 n}{4}\right)+O(n)$ $T(n)=2 T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+O(n)$ $T(n)=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}[T(k)+T(n-k-1)]+O(n)$

Which of the following statements is/are true about the Binary Tree ${T}?$

  1. Node $\text{P}$ is the root of $T$
  2. The Post-order traversal of $T$ is:

\begin{array}{lllllll}
S & E & Q & F & G & R & P
\end{array}

questions.explanation: Pre-order: P Q S E R F G   In-order:  S Q E P F R G   In Pre-order, the first element is always the root. questions.questionText: Consider a directed graph $G=(V, E)$, where $V$ is the finite set of vertices and $E$ is the set of directed edges between the vertices. $G$ may contain cycles but there is no self-loop. Further, $G$ may not be strongly connected. Let $G^{R}$ be the graph obtained by reversing the directions of all the edges in $G$ without changing the set of vertices. Assume that Breadth First Search (BFS) or Depth First Search (DFS) from any given vertex $v$ of a graph visits only the reachable vertices from $v$ in that graph. Which of the following statements must always be true, regardless of the structure of ${G}?$ If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$, then $u$ is also a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$. In $G^{R}$, the BFS traversal from $v$ will visit exactly the same set of vertices as the DFS from $v$ in $G$. The order of vertices visited in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$ is the reverse of the order of vertices visited in the DFS of $G$ from $v$. If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$, then $v$ is also a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $u$.
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a directed graph $G=(V, E)$, where $V$ is the finite set of vertices and $E$ is the set of directed edges between the vertices. $G$ may contain cycles but there is no self-loop. Further, $G$ may not be strongly connected.

Let $G^{R}$ be the graph obtained by reversing the directions of all the edges in $G$ without changing the set of vertices.
Assume that Breadth First Search (BFS) or Depth First Search (DFS) from any given vertex $v$ of a graph visits only the reachable vertices from $v$ in that graph.

Which of the following statements must always be true, regardless of the structure of ${G}?$

  1. If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$, then $u$ is also a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.
  2. In $G^{R}$, the BFS traversal from $v$ will visit exactly the same set of vertices as the DFS from $v$ in $G$.
  3. The order of vertices visited in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$ is the reverse of the order of vertices visited in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.
  4. If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$, then $v$ is also a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $u$.

options.label: A
options.text: If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$, then $u$ is also a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.

options.label: B
options.text: In $G^{R}$, the BFS traversal from $v$ will visit exactly the same set of vertices as the DFS from $v$ in $G$.

options.label: C
options.text: The order of vertices visited in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $v$ is the reverse of the order of vertices visited in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.

options.label: D
options.text: If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$, then $v$ is also a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^{R}$ from $u$.

Let $\text{N1}$ be the total number of comparisons done by $\text{BS}$ on the elements of $\text{P}$ and $\text{N2}$ be the total number of comparisons done by $\text{IS}$ on the elements of $\text{P}$. Which of the following options is/are correct? $\mathrm{N} 1=10, \mathrm{~N} 2=4$ $\mathrm{N} 1>\mathrm{N} 2$ $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will perform only one swap Both $\text{BS}$ and $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will make at least one unnecessary comparison (i.e., comparing elements that are already in correct order)
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the problem of sorting the given array in ascending order:

\[
P=[1,2,3,5,4]
\]
Consider two sorting algorithms Bubble Sort $\text{(BS)}$ and Insertion Sort $\text{(IS)}$.
Let $\text{N1}$ be the total number of comparisons done by $\text{BS}$ on the elements of $\text{P}$ and $\text{N2}$ be the total number of comparisons done by $\text{IS}$ on the elements of $\text{P}$.

Which of the following options is/are correct?

  1. $\mathrm{N} 1=10, \mathrm{~N} 2=4$
  2. $\mathrm{N} 1>\mathrm{N} 2$
  3. $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will perform only one swap
  4. Both $\text{BS}$ and $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will make at least one unnecessary comparison (i.e., comparing elements that are already in correct order)

options.label: C
options.text: $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will perform only one swap

options.label: D
options.text: Both $\text{BS}$ and $\text{IS}$ on $\text{P}$ will make at least one unnecessary comparison (i.e., comparing elements that are already in correct order)

questions.explanation: Given array: \[ P = [1,2,3,5,4] \] Only the last two elements are misplaced. Number of elements: \[ n = 5 \] Bubble Sort: For standard Bubble Sort (without early stopping), the total number of comparisons is \[ N_1 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \] \[ N_1 = \frac{5 \cdot 4}{2} = 10 \] Insertion Sort: We count comparisons pass by pass. \[ [1,2,3,5,4] \] i = 1: compare 2 with 1 → 1 comparison   i = 2: compare 3 with 2 → 1 comparison   i = 3: compare 5 with 3 → 1 comparison   i = 4: compare 4 with 5 → 1 comparison i = 5: compare 4 with 3 → 1 comparison   Total comparisons: \[ N_2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 5 \] Thus, \[ N_1 = 10, \quad N_2 = 5 \] Checking options: (A) \( N_1 = 10, N_2 = 4 \) False since \( N_2 = 5 \) (B) \( N_1 > N_2 \) \[ 10 > 5 \] True (C) Insertion Sort performs only one swap. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether $A$ satisfies the condition given below. $\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$ such that $i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])$ Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem? $\Theta(n)$ $\Theta(\log (n))$ $\Theta(n \log (n))$ $\Theta\left(n^{2}\right)$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider an array $A$ of integers of size $n$. The indices of $A$ run from $1$ to $n$. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether $A$ satisfies the condition given below.

$\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$ such that $i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])$

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?

  1. $\Theta(n)$
  2. $\Theta(\log (n))$
  3. $\Theta(n \log (n))$
  4. $\Theta\left(n^{2}\right)$
questions.explanation: The problem asks for the fastest algorithm to check the following condition for an array $A$ of size $n$: $$\forall i, j \in \{1, \dots, n-1\} \text{ such that } i > j, (A[i+1] - A[i]) > (A[j+1] - A[j])$$ Analysis of the Condition The condition essentially states that the difference between adjacent elements must be strictly increasing as we move through the array. Let $D[i] = A[i+1] - A[i]$ for $i = 1, \dots, n-1$. The condition simplifies to: $D[n-1] > D[n-2] > \dots > D[1]$. Complexity Determination To verify this condition, an algorithm must check if every adjacent difference is larger than the previous one: Calculate $D[1] = A[2] - A[1]$. Calculate $D[2] = A[3] - A[2]$ and check if $D[2] > D[1]$. Continue this for all $n-1$ differences. Since you must examine every element of the array at least once to ensure the condition holds globally, the algorithm requires linear time . Algorithm $B_{1}$ : For $i=1,2, \ldots, n$ \[ \begin{array}{l} \text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\ \qquad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] \end{array} \] Algorithm $B_{2}:$ For $s=2,3, \ldots, 2 n$ \[ \begin{array}{l} \text { For } i=1,2, \ldots, n \\ \qquad \begin{array}{l} \text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\ \qquad \text { If }(i+j==s) \\ \quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] \end{array} \end{array} \] Algorithm $B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}$ is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of $T[i][j]$, for all $0 \leq i, j \leq n$, (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm $B_{k}$. Which one of the following statements is true? Both algorithms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are correct Algorithm $B_{1}$ is correct, but algorithm $B_{2}$ is incorrect Algorithm $B_{2}$ is correct, but algorithm $B_{1}$ is incorrect Both algorithms $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are incorrect

Consider a table $T$, where the elements $T[i][j], 0 \leq i, j \leq n$, represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\
T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n
\end{array}
\]
Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of $T$. Assume that for both the algorithms, for all $0 \leq i, j \leq n, T[i][j]$ has been initialized to $1$.
Algorithm $B_{1}$ : For $i=1,2, \ldots, n$
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\qquad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1]
\end{array}
\]
Algorithm $B_{2}:$ For $s=2,3, \ldots, 2 n$
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text { For } i=1,2, \ldots, n \\

\text { For } j=1,2, \ldots, n \\
\qquad \text { If }(i+j==s) \\
\quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1]
\end{array}
\end{array}
\]
Algorithm $B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}$ is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of $T[i][j]$, for all $0 \leq i, j \leq n$, (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm $B_{k}$.

questions.questionText: Consider a binary search tree (BST) with $n$ leaf nodes $(n>0)$. Given any node $V$, the key present in the node is denoted as $\operatorname{Val}(V)$. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers. For a node $V$, let $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node $V$ does not have an inorder successor, then $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ is $N U L L$. As there are no duplicates, if $\operatorname{Suc}(V)$ is not $N U L L$, then $\operatorname{Val}(V)<\operatorname{Val}(\operatorname{Suc}(V))$. Corresponding to every leaf node $L_{i}$ that has a non-NULL $\operatorname{Suc}\left(L_{i}\right)$, a new key $k_{i}$ with the following property is to be inserted into the BST. \[ \operatorname{Val}\left(L_{i}\right)  < k_{i} < Val (\operatorname{Suc}(L_{i}))\] Let $K$ represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST. Which of the following statements is/are true? $K$ cannot have any duplicates $K$ will have at least one element After inserting all keys from $K$, the height of the BST can increase at most by one Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from $K$

questions.explanation: we know that for  any binary tree: total number of nodes $n$= internal nodes $(I)$+ leaf node $( L)$ In a Full Binary Tree , the number of leaves is always one more than the internal nodes:$L=I+1$ Substitute $L$ into the total nodes equation:  $n = I + (I + 1) = 2I + 1$ now put $n = 23$:  $23 = 2I + 1 \implies 22 = 2I \implies I = 11$. To get the maximum height , we should arrange these$11$ internal nodes in a single path (skew tree). Each internal node then contributes exactly 1 edge to the height.Therefore, Max Height = Number of Internal Nodes = 11 . questions.explanation: For a BST with $15$ nodes which is also a Complete Binary Tree  there is only one possibility:  Option-A   $\to$ Insert sequence $8 ,4 , 2 \to$ it is possible for $2$ to be the third element to be inserted and still get at the correct position in the above tree. Option-B  (It should be $4$ and not $2$ in the question, printing mistake)  $\to$ Insert sequence $8, 12, 4 \to$ it is possible for $4$ to be the third element to be inserted and still get at the correct position in the above tree. Option-C $\to$ Insert sequence $8,12,10 \to$  it is possible for $10$ to be the third element to be inserted and still get at the correct position in the above tree. Option-D   $\to$ Here no matter what sequence you choose it is not possible to put $5$ at the correct position (last/leaf level of tree) because we only have $2$ elements ahead of it in the sequence which can put $5$ at level-1 or level-2 but not at level-3. Answer: $\boxed{D-5}$

questions.questionText: Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph $G(V, E)$ as input, where $d[v]$ and $f[v]$ are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex $v \in V$. \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|p{7cm}|p{7cm}|} \hline \textbf{DFS}(G):  \begin{array}{l} \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t):  \begin{array}{l} \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} \] Suppose that the input directed graph $G(V, E)$ is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge $(u, v) \in E$, which of the following options will NEVER be correct? $d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u]$ $d[v] < d[u] < f[u]< f[v]$ $d[v] < f[v] < d[u] < f[u]$ $d[u] < d[v] < f[u] < f[v]$

Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph $G(V, E)$ as input, where $d[v]$ and $f[v]$ are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex $v \in V$.

\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{array}{|p{7cm}|p{7cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{DFS}(G): 
\begin{array}{l}
\text{unmark all } v \in V \\
t \leftarrow 0 \\
\text{for each } v \in V \\
\quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\
\qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\
\quad \text{end if} \\
\text{end for}
\end{array}
&
\textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): 
\begin{array}{l}
\text{mark } v \\
t \leftarrow t+1 \\
d[v] \leftarrow t \\
\text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\
\quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\
\qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\
\quad \text{end if} \\
\text{end for} \\
t \leftarrow t+1 \\
f[v] \leftarrow t \\
\text{return } t
\end{array}
\\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

For an edge $(u, v) \in E$, which of the following options will NEVER be correct?

  2. $d[v] < d[u] < f[u]< f[v]$
  3. $d[v] < f[v] < d[u] < f[u]$
  4. $d[u] < d[v] < f[u] < f[v]$

questions.questionText: Combinatorics deals with problems involving counting. For example, "How many distinct arrangements of $\text{N}$ distinct objects in $\text{M}$ spaces on a circle are possible?" is a typical problem in combinatorics. This kind of counting is sometimes used in the modeling of several physical phenomena. Often, in such models, the different combinatorial possibilities are assigned probability values. Assigning probabilities enables the computation of the average values of physical quantities. Consider the following statements: $\text{P}:$ Combinatorics is always invoked in the modeling of physical phenomena. $\text{Q}:$ Modeling some physical phenomena involves assigning probabilities to combinatorial possibilities in order to compute average values of physical quantities. questions.explanation: To find the inference that is NOT necessarily true, we can translate the statement into a logical conditional: $P \implies Q$ $P$ (Condition): The teacher is in the room. $Q$ (Result): All students stand silently. Option A  is the Contrapositive ($\neg Q \implies \neg P$). In formal logic, the contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original statement. If the students are not standing silently (the result is not happening), then the condition that forces them to do so (the teacher's presence) cannot be true. Option B is a direct restatement of the original premise ($P \implies Q$). Since the statement explicitly says students stand when the teacher is in the room, this must be true by definition. Option C  represents the Converse ($Q \implies P$). It assumes that because the students are standing, the teacher must be present. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  2. $f(x)$ has a minimum at $2$ only.

codeBlocks: Hence {B,D} are accurate.
questions.explanation: \[ f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2, \quad x \in (-1,3]. \] 1) Roots of f(x) Method 1: Direct factorization Check x = 1: \[ f(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0. \] So, 1 is a root. Factorizing: \[ f(x) = (x-1)(x^2 - 2x - 2). \] Solve: \[ x^2 - 2x - 2 = 0. \] \[ x = 1 \pm \sqrt{3}. \] Approximate roots: \[ 1-\sqrt{3} \approx -0.732, \quad 1, \quad 1+\sqrt{3} \approx 2.732. \] In the interval [-0.9,0], only one root \[ -0.732 \] exists. Method 2: Using Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) Since f(x) is a polynomial, it is continuous on [-0.9,0]. Check signs: \[ f(-0.9) = -1.159 < 0 \] \[ f(0) = 2 > 0 \] Since the function changes sign, \[ f(-0.9)\cdot f(0) < 0, \] by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there exists at least one root in (-0.9,0). Note: Opposite signs guarantee at least one root, but not necessarily exactly one root. questions.explanation: Given: \[ \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} 2^{-i} 3^{-j}. \] Since the terms are separable: \[ 2^{-i} 3^{-j} = (2^{-i})(3^{-j}), \] we can write the double sum as: \[ \left( \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} 2^{-i} \right) \left( \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} 3^{-j} \right). \] First sum: \[ \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} 2^{-i} = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^i. \] This is a geometric series with first term \(1\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). \[ = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = 2. \] Second sum: \[ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} 3^{-j} = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^j. \] This is a geometric series with first term \(\frac{1}{3}\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{3}\). \[ = \frac{\frac{1}{3}}{1 - \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{1/3}{2/3} = \frac{1}{2}. \] Multiply: \[ 2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1. \] Final Answer: \[ \boxed{1} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 1 1 vote Since $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}$ does

questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.


$\text{S1}$: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

$\text{S2}$: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to  $\text{S1}$ and  $\text{S2}?$

  1. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true
  2. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false
  3. $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false
  4. $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true
questions.explanation: S1: "Non-vectored takes more time to start ISR than vectored" Non-vectored: CPU polls to find source first, then jumps to ISR. Vectored: device sends ISR address directly. So non-vectored has extra polling overhead → S1 is TRUE ✅ S2: "In daisy chain, CPU polls all devices individually" In daisy-chain, the interrupt request line is shared, and devices are connected in a chain. The CPU acknowledges the interrupt, and the signal passes through devices; the first device that needs service grabs it. No polling by CPU; it's hardware-based. → S2 is FALSE ❌ Answer: (C) S1 true, S2 false Gopika_G answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 25 by Misbah Ghaya Gopika_G comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes S1: True In  non-vectored interrupt , CPU does  not know the ISR address directly . Execution Trace (Sequence: P, Q, R, S repeated 10x) Access P: Miss. Block 0x845B3 (containing P and R) is loaded into Index 0xB3 . Access Q: Miss. Block 0x845B2 is loaded into Index 0xB2 . Access R: HIT. Since P and R are in the same block ( 0x845B3 ), R is already in the cache. Access S: Miss. Block 0x846B3 is loaded into Index 0xB3 , evicting the block containing P and R. In every subsequent loop: P will miss (because S evicted it). Q will hit (it has its own index 0xB2 and is never evicted). R will hit (because P just re-loaded the block they share). Since, size of physical memoery is given as 1 MB i.e. 2^20 B. therefore, the Physical address will comprise of 20 Bits. Now, 20 bits will be distributed between Tag, Cache Index and Byte Offset. Binary of 176 is a 8 bit number which fits exactly into 101000 10110000 101000. Therefore, 20 bit number translates to : Tag = 6 bits, Index = 8 Bits, Offset = 6 Bits. Initially, the head is on track $0$. The number of sectors per track is $400$. The sector size is $1024$ bytes. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of $15000$ rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is $1$ millisecond. Initially, the head is on track $0$. The number of sectors per track is $400$. The sector size is $1024$ bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from $10$ randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: $5, 12$ and $7$.

The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation: Given that, Rotation speed $= 15000$ rpm Track-to-track movement time $= 1~ms$ No. of sectors$/$track $= 400$ We need to access $10$ randomly located sectors in each of the tracks $5, 12, 7$. Time for one complete rotation: $R_t = \dfrac{60}{15000}~sec = 0.004~sec = 4~ms$ Average rotational delay: $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2~ms$ $($half of time taken for one rotation$)$ Transfer time for one sector: Since $1$ rotation ($4~ms$) reads $400$ sectors (as there are $400$ sectors in a track), $T_t = \dfrac{4}{400} = 0.01~ms$ Important Point : Since the 10 sectors in each track are randomly located, they can be anywhere on that track. Therefore, after reading one sector, the disk must rotate again to bring the next required sector under the head. Hence, we need to consider average rotational latency for each sector separately, not just once per track. Time per sector $=$ Avg. Rot. Delay $+$ Transfer time $= 2 + 0.01 = 2.01~ms$ Time to read $10$ sectors in one track: $10 \times 2.01 = 20.1~ms$ Initiall

If $L$ has $2$ unique opcodes and $M$ has $7$ unique opcodes, then the number of opcodes possible for $N$ is

  2. $8$
     
  3. $16$
     
  4. $64$

questions.questionText: Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of $\mathbf{15000 ~ rpm}$. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is $1$ millisecond. Initially the head is on track $\mathbf{0}$. The number of sectors per track is $\mathbf{400}$. The sector size is $1024$ bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from 10 randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order $5$, $12$ and $7$. The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$?
questions.questionHtml: Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of $\mathbf{15000 ~ rpm}$. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is $1$ millisecond. Initially the head is on track $\mathbf{0}$. The number of sectors per track is $\mathbf{400}$. The sector size is $1024$ bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from 10 randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order $5$, $12$ and $7$. The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is $\_\_\_\_\_\_$?
questions.explanation: Given that, Rotation speed $= 15000$ rpm Track-to-track movement time $= 1~ms$ No. of sectors$/$track $= 400$ We need to access $10$ randomly located sectors in each of the tracks $5, 12, 7$. Time for one complete rotation: $R_t = \dfrac{60}{15000}~sec = 0.004~sec = 4~ms$ Average rotational delay: $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2~ms$ $($half of time taken for one rotation$)$ Transfer time for one sector: Since $1$ rotation ($4~ms$) reads $400$ sectors (as there are $400$ sectors in a track), $T_t = \dfrac{4}{400} = 0.01~ms$ Important Point : Since the 10 sectors in each track are randomly located, they can be anywhere on that track. Therefore, after reading one sector, the disk must rotate again to bring the next required sector under the head. Hence, we need to consider average rotational latency for each sector separately, not just once per track. Time per sector $=$ Avg. Rot. Delay $+$ Transfer time $= 2 + 0.01 = 2.01~ms$ Time to read $10$ sectors in one track: $10 \times 2.01 = 20.1~ms$ Initiall

questions.questionText: Real-valued variables $X$ and $Y$ are represented in IEEE-754 single precision floating point format.   Binary representations of $X$ and $Y$ are: $$ \begin{aligned} X &= (35C00000)_H\\ Y &= (34A00000)_H \end{aligned} $$ Let $Z = X + Y$. Which of the following is the binary representation of $Z$ (in hexadecimal)? $(35C80000)_H$  $(35E80000)_H$  $(35EC0000)_H$  $(35CC0000)_H$
questions.questionHtml:
Real-valued variables $X$ and $Y$ are represented in IEEE-754 single precision floating point format.  
Binary representations of $X$ and $Y$ are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &= (35C00000)_H\\
Y &= (34A00000)_H
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Z = X + Y$. Which of the following is the binary representation of $Z$ (in hexadecimal)?

  1. $(35C80000)_H$ 
     
  2. $(35E80000)_H$ 
     
  3. $(35EC0000)_H$ 
     
  4. $(35CC0000)_H$
questions.explanation: $X~\&~Y$ are represented in IEEE-754 format.  IEEE-754 Format :  Floating point no. $= (-1)^S\times1.Mantissa \times 2^{(E-127)}$ $X : (35C00000)_H$  Exponent : $(01101011)_b = (107)_d$ $X = (-1)^0 \times 1.1 \times 2^{(107-127)} = \mathbf{1.1 \times2^{-20}}$ $Y : (34A00000)_H$ Exponent $= (01101001)_b = (105)_d$ $Y= (-1)^0 \times 1.01 \times 2^{(105-127)} = 001.01 \times 2^{-22} = \mathbf{0.0101 \times 2^{-20}}$ Adding $X$ and $Y$, we get  $\therefore Z = X+Y = (1.1 \times 2^{-20}) + (0.0101 \times 2^{-20})$ $\therefore Z = 1.1101 \times 2^{-20}$ Converting $Z$ into IEEE-754 format :  Sign bit $= 0$ Biased Exponent $= -20 + 127 = 107 = (01101011)_b$ Mantissa $= 11010000000000000000000$ Combining it into $32$-bit IEEE-754 format : $(0011 ~0101 ~1110 ~1000 ~0000 ~0000 ~0000 ~0000)_b = \mathbf{(35E80000)_h}$ benzene06 answered Feb 13 • edited Feb 13 by benzene06 benzene06 comment Share Follow See 1 comment 1 1 comment reply shahidhope commented Feb 14 r

questions.questionHtml:
Consider a system with the following cache configuration:

Block size $=128$ bytes  

Physical memory size $=2^{23}$ bytes  

Cache size $=2^{13}$ bytes  

Two cache organizations are used:

1. A direct-mapped cache with tag size $=m$ bits.  

2. A $k$-way set associative cache with tag size $=n$ bits where  
\[
k=2^L,\quad L\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}
\]

Which of the following relations between $n$ and $m$ is/are correct?

  1. $n=m-L$  
     
  2. $n=m+L$  
     
  3. $n=mL$  
     
  4. $n=m+k$
questions.explanation: Physical memory = 2^23 B  block size is 128 B so its 7 bits for block offset  cache size = 2^13 B  1) For the direct mapped cache The number of lines will be 2^13 / 2^7 = 2^6 so 6 bits for line index remaining 10 bits so the tag so m = 10  2) For K - way set associative cache  lines will be 2^6 now for number of set we do 2^6 / 2^L = 2^6-L so 6-L bits for set index remaining bits will be for tag which is n = 23 - (6 - L) - 7 = 23 - 6 + L -7 = 10 + L = m + L hence option B is correct n = m + L all other options are wrong

Which of the following statements is/are true?

  1. $\text{LL(1)}$ parser uses backtracking
  2. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-recursive
  3. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-factored
  4. The $\text{LL(1)}$ parsers are more powerful than the SLR parsers

questions.explanation: $\boxed{\text{Answer: C}}$ Watch detailed discussion on this question $\text{LL(1)}$ parser uses backtracking. $\ \textcolor{red}{\boxed{\text{False}}}$ No, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser is a predictive parser. When expanding a nonterminal, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser predict the production to use by looking at the next token of the input. The decision is forced.  So, $\text{LL(1)}$ parser is not using backtracking. For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-recursive. $\ \textcolor{red}{\boxed{\text{False}}}$ No. In fact for a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must not be left-recursive. Since left-recursive grammar can never be $\text{LL(1)}$. Proof1   Proof2 For a grammar to be $\text{LL(1)}$, it must be left-factored. $\ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{\text{True}}}$ Yes, because non-left-factored grammar can never be $\text{LL(1)}$. questions.excerpt: Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ for type declarations.\[\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}\begin{array}{|l|l|}\hline...
questions.questionText: Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ for type declarations. \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD1}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_1) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow TV & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ V.type = T.type \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} V_1.type = V.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline V \rightarrow \text{id} & \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \\ \hline \end{array} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD2}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_2) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow D_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = D_1.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, D_1.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, T.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline \end{array} \] $D$ is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal $V_{1}$ is the same as $V$ and the non-terminal $D_{1}$ is the same as $D$. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier. Let $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ be the languages specified by grammars $\text{G1}$ and $\text{G2}$, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true? The languages $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ are the same $\text{SDD2}$ is $\text{S}$-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes $\text{SDD1}$ is $\text{L}$-attributed and contains only inherited attributes The specifications of $\text{SDD1}$ and $\text{SDD2}$ are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

questions.questionText: Q. Consider the following two SDDs. SDD1 $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Grammar} & \textbf{Semantic\ Rule} \\ \hline D \rightarrow TV & D.type = T.type \\ & V.type = T.type \\ \hline T \rightarrow int & T.type = int \\ \hline T \rightarrow float & T.type = float \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\, id & V.type = V_1.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;V_1.type) \\ \hline V \rightarrow id & Put(id.entry,\;V.type) \\ \hline \end{array} $$ SDD2 $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Grammar} & \textbf{Semantic\ Rule} \\ \hline D \rightarrow D_1\, id & D.type = D_1.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;D_1.type) \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\, id & D.type = T.type \\ & Put(id.entry,\;T.type) \\ \hline T \rightarrow int & T.type = int \\ \hline T \rightarrow float & T.type = float \\ \hline \end{array} $$ Which of the following is/are correct?  SDD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes. Both SDDs generate the same language. SDD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes. The specifications of SDD1 and SDD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table.

For the input string \[ \texttt{x1 23mm 78 y 7z z25 14A 8H AaycD} \] how many tokens are generated by the lexical analyzer excluding whitespace ?
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a lexical analyzer with the following token specifications:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{letter} &\rightarrow \texttt{[A-Z a-z]} \\
\texttt{digit}  &\rightarrow \texttt{[0-9]} \\
\texttt{id}     &\rightarrow \texttt{letter}\texttt{[letter}\mid \texttt{digit]}^{*} \\
\texttt{no}     &\rightarrow \texttt{[digit]}^{+} \\
\texttt{ws}     &\rightarrow \texttt{[blank}\mid \texttt{tab}\mid \texttt{newline]}^{+}
\end{aligned}
\]

All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file. Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file? Note: $1 \mathrm{M}=10^{6}, 1 \mathrm{k}=10^{3}$ $731$ $64$ $8$ $16$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a file of size $4$ million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth $2$ Mbps , $500$ kbps , and $1$ Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.


Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?

Note: $1 \mathrm{M}=10^{6}, 1 \mathrm{k}=10^{3}$

  1. $731$
  2. $64$
  3. $8$
  4. $16$
codeBlocks:
Bottleneck = min(2 Mbps, 500 kbps, 1 Mbps) = 500 kbps
File size = 4 × 10⁶ × 8 = 32 × 10⁶ bits
Time = 32 × 10⁶ / (500 × 10³) = 64 seconds

questions.questionHtml:
With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which of the following statements is/are true? 

  1. The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer.
     
  2. A TCP connection is half-duplex. 
     
  3. The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time. 
     
  4. The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates.

options.label: A
options.text: The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer.

options.label: C
options.text: The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates.

questions.explanation: Option-$\mathbf{A}$ The client and the server use a $2$-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transfer. Ans : False Reason : Before data transfer, TCP establishes the connection using a $3$-way handshake by exchanging SYN, SYN+ACK, and ACK segments. Option-$\mathbf{B}$ A TCP connection is half-duplex. Ans : False Reason : TCP offers full-duplex service. source: forouzan Option- $\mathbf{C}$ The client and the server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time. Ans : True Reason : Both the ends of TCP connection may send FIN segments at the same time. source: tanenbaum Option- $\mathbf{D}$ The sever cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates. Ans : False Reason : TCP connection release can be initiated by either side (client or server). source: forouzan Answer : $\mathbf{(C)}$ benzene06 answered Feb 16 benzene06 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: Let $\text{R(A, B, C, D, E)}$ be a relational schema with functional dependency set $\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\}$. Which of the following statements is correct? $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$. $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$. $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$. $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\text{R(A, B, C, D, E)}$ be a relational schema with functional dependency set $\mathrm{F}=\{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}\}$.

Which of the following statements is correct?

  1. $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
  2. $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$.
  3. $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.
  4. $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: A
options.text: $\text{AD, ED}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: B
options.text: $\text{AD}$ and $\text{ED}$ are the only candidate keys of $\mathrm{R}$.

options.label: C
options.text: $\text{A, E}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

options.label: D
options.text: $\text{A}$ and $\text{CD}$ are the only candidate keys of $\text{R}$.

questions.explanation: This is a basic fundamental question. To save time, we have  an important property: Any attribute that does NOT appear on the RHS of any functional dependency must be present in every candidate key. Given: \[ F = \{ A \to BC,\; CD \to E,\; E \to A \} \] RHS attributes = {B, C, E, A} Attribute \(D\) does NOT appear on the RHS. Hence, \(D\) must be present in every candidate key. Now eliminate options that do not contain \(D\). Remaining possibilities: \(AD, ED, CD\) Check closures: \[ (AD)^+ = ABCDE \] \[ (ED)^+ = ABCDE \] \[ (CD)^+ = ABCDE \] Thus, the only candidate keys are: \[ AD,\; ED,\; CD \] Correct option: \[ {(A)} \]

questions.questionText: In a relational database, a $\mathrm{B}+$ Tree Index is to be constructed for a relation on a key field. In a $\text{B+}$ Tree, a Node Pointer points to a sub-tree and a Data Record Pointer points to a block of database records. Let, Node size $=4096$ bytes, Node Pointer size $=10$ bytes, Search Key Field size $=11$ bytes and Data Record Pointer size $= 12$ bytes. The maximum number of Node Pointers that can be present in a non-leaf node of the $\text{B+}$ Tree is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.questionHtml:
In a relational database, a $\mathrm{B}+$ Tree Index is to be constructed for a relation on a key field. In a $\text{B+}$ Tree, a Node Pointer points to a sub-tree and a Data Record Pointer points to a block of database records.

Let, Node size $=4096$ bytes, Node Pointer size $=10$ bytes, Search Key Field size $=11$ bytes and Data Record Pointer size $= 12$ bytes.

The maximum number of Node Pointers that can be present in a non-leaf node of the $\text{B+}$ Tree is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Given: Block size = 4096 bytes   Node pointer size = 10 bytes   Search key size = 11 bytes   For a non-leaf node: If there are p node pointers, then there are (p - 1) search keys. Total size condition: \[ 10p + 11(p - 1) \le \lfloor 4096 \rfloor \] Expand: \[ 10p + 11p - 11 \le 4096 \] \[ 21p - 11 \le 4096 \] \[ 21p \le 4107 \] \[ p \le \frac{4107}{21} \] \[ p \le 195.57 \] Taking floor: \[ p = \left\lfloor \frac{4107}{21} \right\rfloor = 195 \] Final Answer: \[ \boxed{195} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 23 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Consider a B+ Tree where the maximum number of key values in each leaf node is $2$ and the maximum number of pointers in each non-leaf node is $3$. Let the content of the B+ Tree be as shown in the figure.

Which of the following options denotes the key value(s) stored in the root node after inserting a key value $3$ in the given B+ Tree?

  1. $5$
  2. $8$
  3. $3$ and $5$
  4. $3, 5$ and $8$
questions.explanation: Note: In this question, we are not required to draw Full B+ tree to save time. Maximum keys in each leaf node = 2 Maximum pointers in each internal node = 3 Maximum keys in each internal node = 2 In a B+tree , we know that insertion always happens at root node.   Root: \[ [5 , 8] \] Leaf Nodes: \[ [1,5] \rightarrow [7,8] \rightarrow [9,12] \] Insert key = 3 Since $3 < 5$, it is inserted in the first leaf node: \[ [1,5] \Rightarrow [1,3,5] \] But a leaf can contain at most 2 keys.   Hence, overflow occurs and the node must be split. Split the leaf node: \[ [1,3,5] \Rightarrow [1,3] \quad \text{and} \quad [5] \]   Root becomes: \[ [3,5,8] \] Now the root has 3 keys, but it can hold at most 2 keys.   Hence, root overflow occurs. Split the root: \[ [3,5,8] \] Middle key $5$ moves up and becomes the new root. Final Root \[ \boxed{5} \] Correct Option: (A)

Which of the following is/are correct? \[ \textbf{Employee} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamID} \\ \hline 1 & 8 \\ \hline 2 & 8 \\ \hline 3 & 8 \\ \hline 4 & 7 \\ \hline 5 & 7 \\ \hline 6 & 9 \\ \hline \end{array} \] \[ \textbf{Output} \] \[ \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3} \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{EmpID} & \text{TeamSize} \\ \hline 1 & 3 \\ \hline 2 & 3 \\ \hline 3 & 3 \\ \hline 4 & 2 \\ \hline 5 & 2 \\ \hline 6 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array} \] SELECT E.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM Employee AS E, (SELECT TeamID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B WHERE E.TeamID = B.TeamID SELECT A.EmpID, COUNT(B.TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, Employee AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID AND A.EmpID = B.EmpID GROUP BY A.EmpID SELECT B.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM (SELECT EmpID, COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY EmpID) AS B SELECT A.EmpID, B.TeamSize FROM Employee AS A, (SELECT COUNT(TeamID) AS TeamSize FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) AS B WHERE A.TeamID = B.TeamID

questions.explanation: In this question, we need to focus on the attributes used in the GROUP BY clause. Since we are asked to find the team size, the grouping must be done based on TeamID , not EmpID . Options B and C are clearly incorrect because they group by EmpID , whereas the requirement is to group rows based on TeamID . Team size is obtained by grouping on TeamID and applying COUNT(column_name) to get the number of employees in each team. When it comes to option D, the issue is that there is no TeamID present in the inner query result. Because of this, it is not possible to match with the condition A.TeamID = B.TeamID after the cross product, making the query invalid. Finally, option A works correctly because the inner query provides the necessary TeamID , which allows proper matching after the cross product and results in the correct team size for each employee.

questions.questionHtml:
Consider concurrent execution of two transactions $T 1$ and $T 2$ in a DBMS, both of which access a data object $A$. For these two transactions to not conflict on $A$, which one of the following statements must be true?

  1. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ only read $A$
  2. $T 1$ reads $A$ and $T 2$ writes $A$
  3. $T 1$ writes $A$ and $T 2$ reads $A$
  4. Both $T 1$ and $T 2$ write $A$
questions.explanation: Answer: Option A In a DBMS, two operations on the same data object Q are said to be in conflict if at least one of them is a Write operation. Conflict Conditions For two transactions T1 and T2 accessing the same data object Q are said to be in conflict if at least one of them is a Write operation. Read-Read (R-R): No Conflict. Both transactions are only viewing the data; the state of $Q$ remains unchanged. Read-Write (R-W): Conflict. One transaction reads while the other updates, leading to potential inconsistency. Write-Read (W-R): Conflict. Known as a "Dirty Read" if the write hasn't been committed. Write-Write (W-W): Conflict. Known as a "Blind Write" or "Lost Update" problem. Therefore, for T1 and T2 to not conflict , the only valid scenario is when both T1 and T2 only read Q. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/concurrency-control-in-dbms/  akash_kumar 9 answered Feb 25 akash_kumar 9 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Although I

questions.questionText: In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $\text{F}$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $\text{F}$ is called the closure of $\text{F}$. To compute the closure of $\text{F}$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X, Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows. Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$ Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $X Z \rightarrow Y Z$ for any Z Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$ The additional rule of Union is defined as follows. Union: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Y Z$ It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof? Reflexivity, Augmentation, and Transitivity Reflexivity and Augmentation Transitivity Augmentation and Transitivity
questions.questionHtml:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $\text{F}$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $\text{F}$ is called the closure of $\text{F}$. To compute the closure of $\text{F}$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X, Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$

Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $X Z \rightarrow Y Z$ for any Z

Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Y Z$

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?

  1. Reflexivity, Augmentation, and Transitivity
  2. Reflexivity and Augmentation
  3. Transitivity
  4. Augmentation and Transitivity
questions.explanation: Answer : D We know $X \to Y$. $X \to Y$ with $X$ itself. Found: $XX \to XY$, simplify to $X \to XY$ . We know $X \to Z$. $X \to Z$ with $Y$. Result: $XY \to YZ$ . Since we have $X \to XY$ and $XY \to YZ$. UNION: $X \to YZ$ . Srinivas_Chundi answered Mar 3 Srinivas_Chundi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.


$\text{S1}$: A hash index must be a dense index
$\text{S1}$: A $B^{+}$ tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?

  1. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are true
  2. Both $\text{S1}$ and $\text{S2}$ are false
  3. $\text{S1}$ is true and $\text{S2}$ is false
  4. $\text{S1}$ is false and $\text{S2}$ is true
questions.explanation: S1: A hash index must be a dense index Status: True Reason: Every unique search-key value requires a corresponding entry in the hash table to be located by the hash function. By definition, an index that tracks every search-key value is a dense index . S2: A B+ tree index can be a sparse index Status: True Reason: While B+ trees are often dense, they can be sparse when acting as a primary (clustering) index. In this mode, they only store entries for a subset of keys (usually one per data block), which helps minimize index size. so option A is correct

questions.questionText: Consider a relational database schema with two relations $R(P, Q)$ and $S(X, Y)$. Let $E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}$ be a tuple relational calculus expression. Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to $E$ ? $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . X} S\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . X=R . Q} R\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . Y} S\right)$ $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . Y=R . Q} R\right)$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations $R(P, Q)$ and $S(X, Y)$.

Let $E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}$ be a tuple relational calculus expression.

Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to $E$ ?

  1. $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . X} S\right)$
  2. $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . X=R . Q} R\right)$
  3. $\Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R . P=S . Y} S\right)$
  4. $\Pi_{P}\left(S \bowtie_{S . Y=R . Q} R\right)$
questions.explanation: The expression \( E \) describes a set of tuples \(\langle u \rangle\) such that there exists a tuple \(\langle u, v \rangle\) in relation \( R \) and a tuple \(\langle v, w \rangle\) in relation \( S \). This implies that \( v \) is a common attribute between the two relations, specifically \( R.Q \) and \( S.X \). Now, let's translate this into relational algebra: 1. Join Condition: We need to perform a join between \( R \) and \( S \) on the condition \( R.Q = S.X \) because \( v \) is the common attribute. 2. Projection: After joining, we are interested in the attribute \( P \) from relation \( R \). Therefore, the equivalent relational algebra expression is: \[ \Pi_{P}\left(R \bowtie_{R.Q = S.X} S\right) \] This expression selects the attribute \( P \) from relation \( R \), where \( R.Q = S.X \) in the joined tables, which aligns with the tuple relational calculus expression given in the problem. \[
A \rightarrow BC,\qquad CD \rightarrow E,\qquad E \rightarrow A.
\]
What are the candidate keys of $R$ ?

  2. $\{AC,\; CD,\; DE\}$

  3. $\{AD,\; CE,\; CD\}$

  4. $\{A,\; CD,\; ED\}$
questions.explanation: Answer: (A) {AD, CD, ED} To find the candidate keys, we determine the closure of each potential key attribute set. A set of attributes $X$ is a candidate key if its closure, $X^+$, includes all attributes in $R(A, B, C, D, E)$. The given functional dependencies (FDs) are $A \to BC$, $CD \to E$, and $E \to A$. Note that the image likely has a typo and the third FD should be $E \to A$. Check A: $AD^+ = \{A, D\}$ (start with A and D) $A \to BC$, so add B and C: $\{A, B, C, D\}$ $CD \to E$, so add E: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $AD$ is a candidate key. Check CD: $CD^+ = \{C, D\}$ (start with C and D) $CD \to E$, so add E: $\{C, D, E\}$ $E \to A$, so add A: $\{A, C, D, E\}$ $A \to BC$, so add B: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $CD$ is a candidate key. Check ED: $ED^+ = \{E, D\}$ (start with E and D) $E \to A$, so add A: $\{A, D, E\}$ $A \to BC$, so add B and C: $\{A, B, C, D, E\}$ $ED$ is a candidate key. questions.questionHtml:
Consider two relations: $$R(A, B), \quad \quad S(E, C)$$Attribute $A$ is the primary key of relation $R$.  

Attribute $E$ in relation $S$ is a foreign key that references $A$ in $R$.

Which of the following operations will NEVER violate the foreign key constraint?

  1. Delete a record from $R$
     
  2. Delete a record from $S$
     
  3. Insert a record into $R$
     
  4. Insert a record into $S$
questions.explanation: Answer: (B) Delete a record from S & (C) Insert a record into R Explanation (A) Delete a record from R: This operation can violate the foreign key constraint if the record being deleted from table R has its primary key value referenced by one or more records in table S. (B) Delete a record from S: Deleting a record from the referencing table S does not violate the constraint because it removes a reference to a primary key value in R. The referenced value in R still exists. (C) Insert a record into R: Inserting a new record into the referenced table R does not violate the constraint because it introduces a new primary key value that can be referenced by records in S in the future. (D) Insert a record into S: This operation can violate the foreign key constraint if the value inserted into attribute E (the foreign key) does not already exist as a primary key value in attribute A of table R. questions.questionHtml:
In the question, the following three of Armstrong's axioms are given:
Reflexivity (Trivial), Augmentation, and Transitivity.

Now, we want to prove that
$$
\{X \rightarrow Y,\; X \rightarrow Z\} \Rightarrow X \rightarrow YZ
$$
using only the above three Armstrong's axioms.

Use the minimum number of axioms from the given three to prove the result.
Which of the following options can prove the result?

  1. Reflexivity, Transitivity
     
  2. Reflexivity, Augmentation
     
  3. Transitivity, Augmentation
     
  4. Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity
questions.explanation: The Problem We need to prove the Union Rule : $$\{ X \rightarrow Y, X \rightarrow Z \} \Rightarrow X \rightarrow YZ$$ Using the minimum number of Armstrong's Axioms from this list: Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \rightarrow Y$. Augmentation: If $X \rightarrow Y$, then $XZ \rightarrow YZ$. Transitivity: If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$, then $X \rightarrow Z$. Step-by-Step Solution To prove $X \rightarrow YZ$ from the given $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$: Apply Augmentation: Take the given $X \rightarrow Y$. Augment both sides with $X$. Result: $XX \rightarrow XY$, which simplifies to $X \rightarrow XY$ . Apply Augmentation again: Take the given $X \rightarrow Z$. Augment both sides with $Y$. Result: $XY \rightarrow YZ$ . Apply Transitivity: Now we have $X \rightarrow XY$ (from step 1) and $XY \rightarrow YZ$ (from step 2). By transitivity: $X \rightarrow YZ$ . Axioms used: Augmentation, Transitivity. Correct Option: 3. Transitivity, Augmentation

In a dense index, we store an index entry for every record, while in a sparse index we do not store an index entry for every record. Which of the following is true regarding the given two statements? $\mathrm{S1}:$ Hash index MUST have dense indexing. $\mathrm{S2}:$ B+ tree can have sparse index. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are true $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are false $\mathrm{S1}$ is true, $\mathrm{S2}$ is false $\mathrm{S1}$ is false, $\mathrm{S2}$ is true
questions.questionHtml:
In indexing, we have two types of index: Dense Index and Sparse Index.
In a dense index, we store an index entry for every record, while in a sparse index we do not store an index entry for every record. Which of the following is true regarding the given two statements?

$\mathrm{S1}:$ Hash index MUST have dense indexing.

$\mathrm{S2}:$ B+ tree can have sparse index.
 

  1. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are true
     
  2. $\mathrm{S1}$, $\mathrm{S2}$ both are false
     
  3. $\mathrm{S1}$ is true, $\mathrm{S2}$ is false
     
  4. $\mathrm{S1}$ is false, $\mathrm{S2}$ is true
questions.explanation: Option A: S1, S2 both are true Statement 1: Hash index MUST have dense indexing. This statement is generally considered  true  in the context of database indexing fundamentals. A hash index uses a hash function to directly map a search key to a specific "bucket" (which might be a disk block). For efficient retrieval, every search key value generally needs to have an entry in the hash structure to ensure the correct bucket can be found quickly. The hash index typically stores all search keys and their pointers, fitting the definition of a dense index. If it were sparse, the collision handling and search efficiency would be severely degraded, effectively requiring a linear scan within large buckets which defeats the purpose of hashing for speed. Statement 2: B+ tree can have sparse index. This statement is  true . B+ trees are commonly used for multi-level indexing. The non-leaf (internal) nodes in a B+ tree inherently form a hierarchy of sparse indexes on the leaf nodes.

questions.explanation: Given Disk size = 2^34 bytes Block size = 2^11 bytes Total number of blocks 2^34 / 2^11 = 2^23 So total blocks = 2^23 . questions.questionHtml:
Question 9

Let R(A) be a relation that contains both integer and NULL values in attribute A.

Consider the following two queries:

Query 1:

SELECT * FROM R WHERE A NOT IN (5, 10, NULL);

Query 2:

SELECT * FROM R WHERE A <> 5 AND A <> 10 AND A IS NOT NULL;

Which of the following statements is/are false?

A. Query 1 and Query 2 return same tuples.
B. Query 1 will not return any tuple for any value of A.
C. Query 1 returns rows where A is not NULL and is neither 5 nor 10.
D. Query 2 will return all rows where A is neither 5 nor 10.

options.label: A
options.text: Query 1 and Query 2 return same tuples.

options.label: B
options.text: Query 1 will not return any tuple for any value of

options.label: C
options.text: Query 1 returns rows where A is not NULL and is neither 5 nor 10.

options.label: D
options.text: Query 2 will return all rows where A is neither 5 nor 10.

questions.explanation: Answer - A, C The expression  A NOT IN (5, 10, NULL) is equivalent to (A <> 5) AND (A <> 10) AND (A <> NULL). Query 1: But A <> NULL always yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Because the overall condition uses AND, the entire predicate becomes UNKNOWN for every row. UNKNOWN acts as FALSE in the WHERE clause. Therefore, Query 1 returns no rows at all (for any value of A). Query 2: A <> 5 AND A <> 10 AND A IS NOT NULL → This correctly returns rows where A is neither 5 nor 10 and also not NULL.

questions.questionText: Consider a Binary Search Tree (BST) in which all keys are distinct. For a node $v_i$, let $\text{succ}(v_i)$ denote its in-order successor. If $v_i$ has no in-order successor, then $\text{succ}(v_i) = \text{NULL}$. Define a set $K$ as follows: For every leaf node $v_i$ such that $\text{succ}(v_i) \ne \text{NULL}$, choose a key $k_i$ satisfying \[ \text{val}(v_i) < k_i < \text{val}(\text{succ}(v_i)) \] and include $k_i$ in $K$. $($Assume such a key can be chosen whenever $\text{succ}(v_i) \ne \text{NULL})$. Now, insert all keys of $K$ into the given BST (in any order), maintaining the BST property. Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true? $K$ contains no duplicate keys. After inserting all keys from $K$, the height of the BST increases by at most $1$. After inserting all keys from $K$, the number of nodes in the BST becomes exactly double. The set $K$ is non-empty (contains at least one key).

Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true?

  4. The set $K$ is non-empty (contains at least one key).

The Core Concept: 2-Colorable Graphs A graph is 2-colorable if you can assign one of two colors (like $0$ and $1$) to each vertex such that no two connected vertices share the same color. In graph theory, a 2-colorable graph is perfectly equivalent to a Bipartite Graph . The fundamental theorem of bipartite graphs states: A graph is bipartite (2-colorable) if and only if it does NOT contain any cycles of odd length. Evaluating the Options A. Let $M=\left(\begin{array}{rr}\cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta\end{array}\right)$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix, where $\theta=\frac{2 \pi}{5}$, and $I_{2}=\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right)$.

Which of the following options is equal to $M^{2026}$ ?

  1. $M^{2}$
  2. $M$
  3. $M^{-1}$
  4. $I_{2}$
questions.explanation: Given, \[ M = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}. \] This matrix represents rotation by angle \(\theta\). If we multiply rotation matrices, the angles add So, \[ M^k \text{ represents rotation by } k\theta. \] Now, \[ M^5 \text{ represents rotation by } 5\theta. \] But, \[ 5\theta = 5 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{5} = 2\pi. \] Rotation by \(2\pi\) brings us back to the same position. Hence, \[ M^5 = I_2. \] So, we can write 2026 as: \[ 2026 = 5 \times 405 + 1. \] So, \[ M^{2026} = M^{5 \times 405 + 1}. \] \[ = (M^5)^{405} \cdot M. \] \[ = I_2^{405} \cdot M. \] \[ = M. \] Therefore, \[ \boxed{M^{2026} = M}. \] Correct option: \[ {(B)} \]

Let $S_{2}$ be another set which is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with dimension two. Which of the following gives the area of $S_{1} \cap S_{2}$ ? $16 \pi$ $4 \pi$ $4 \pi^{2}$ $16 \pi^{2}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a set $S_{1}=\left\{x=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{3} \mid x^{T} x \leq 16\right\}$. Let $S_{2}$ be another set which is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with dimension two.

Which of the following gives the area of $S_{1} \cap S_{2}$ ?

  1. $16 \pi$
  2. $4 \pi$
  3. $4 \pi^{2}$
  4. $16 \pi^{2}$
questions.explanation: Given: \[ S_1 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x^T x \le 16\}. \] Now, \[ x^T x = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2. \] So the condition becomes: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 \le 16. \] General equation of a sphere centered at origin: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 = r^2. \] Comparing with: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 = 16, \] we get: \[ r^2 = 16. \] Hence, \[ r = \sqrt{16} = 4. \] Also, \[ x^T x = \|x\|^2, \] so the condition \[ x^T x \le 16 \] means \[ \|x\| \le 4, \] i.e., all points whose distance from origin is at most 4. Thus, \(S_1\) is a solid sphere of radius 4 centered at the origin. Since \(S_2\) is a 2-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), it represents a plane passing through the origin. The intersection of a sphere and a plane passing through its center is a circle of the same radius. Therefore, the required area is: \[ \pi r^2 = \pi (4)^2 = 16\pi. \] Hence, \[ \boxed{16\pi}. \] Correct option: \[ {(A)} \]

Which one of the following options lists all the possible values of $t$ satisfying $\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=1+\sqrt{2}$?

  1. $\left\{\frac{\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{4}\right\}$
  2. $\left\{\frac{\pi}{4},-\frac{\pi}{3}\right\}$
  3. $\left\{\frac{\pi}{4},-\frac{\pi}{4}\right\}$
  4. $\left\{\frac{\pi}{3},-\frac{\pi}{3}\right\}$
questions.explanation: Given the matrix \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos t & \sin t \\ 0 & -\sin t & \cos t \end{bmatrix} \] We know that: \[ \text{Sum of eigenvalues} = \operatorname{tr}(A) \] The trace of the matrix is the sum of its diagonal elements: \[ \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1 + \cos t + \cos t = 1 + 2\cos t \] Given: \[ \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 = 1 + \sqrt{2} \] Since the sum of eigenvalues equals the trace: \[ 1 + 2\cos t = 1 + \sqrt{2} \] Subtracting 1 from both sides: \[ 2\cos t = \sqrt{2} \] \[ \cos t = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \] So, \[ \cos t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \] We know that cosine is an even function, i.e., \[ \cos(-t) = \cos(t) \] For \( t \in [-\pi, \pi] \), \[ t = \frac{\pi}{4}, \quad -\frac{\pi}{4} \] \[ \boxed{\left\{ \frac{\pi}{4}, -\frac{\pi}{4} \right\}} \] \[ \textbf{Correct Option: (C)} \]

questions.explanation: The system is: $$ax + y = b$$ $$16x + ay = 24$$ The augmented matrix is: $$[A|B] = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 & | & b \\ 16 & a & | & 24 \end{bmatrix}$$ Row Reduction (Gaussian Elimination) $$\begin{bmatrix} a & 1 & | & b \\ 0 & a^2 - 16 & | & 24a - 16b \end{bmatrix}$$ For the system to have  infinite solutions , the rank must be  1 .  Therefore, both terms in the second row must be zero: Condition 1 (Coefficient part must be 0): $$a^2 - 16 = 0$$ $$a = \pm 4$$ Condition 2 (Augmented part must be 0): $$24a - 16b = 0$$ $$3a - 2b = 0 \implies 3a = 2b$$ Case 1: If $a = 4$ $$3(4) = 2b$$ $$12 = 2b \implies b = 6$$ Product $ab = 4 \times 6 = 24$ Case 2: If $a = -4$ $$3(-4) = 2b$$ $$-12 = 2b \implies b = -6$$ Product $ab = (-4) \times (-6) = 24$ Answer: In both cases, the product is  24 . questions.explanation: False Statements Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks Explanation: This is false because the Banker's algorithm is used for Deadlock Avoidance , not prevention. Prevention involves negating one of the four necessary conditions (like Hold and Wait), while Avoidance dynamically checks for a safe sequence. An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource Explanation: This is false. In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), an Assignment Edge goes from Resource $\rightarrow$ Process , showing the resource is held. An edge from Process $\rightarrow$ Resource is a Request Edge . True Statements Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed Explanation: True. Forcing a process to request all resources at once (or only when it has none) breaks the "Hold and Wait" condition, effectively preventing deadlocks. questions.explanation: The Deadlock-Free Formula The standard formula for a system with $n$ processes and a single resource type where each process P has a maximum requirement m is: Step-by-Step Calculation Identify the variables: * Number of processes (n) = 5. Maximum requirement for each process (m) = 2. Calculate the "Worst-Case" allocation: A deadlock occurs if every process holds one less than its maximum requirement and no resources are left. Each process holds (2 - 1) = 1 instance. Total instances held by all 5 processes in this state = 5 *1 = 5. Find the minimum k: To break the deadlock, you need at least one more resource so that one process can finish. k = 5 + 1 = 6. Final Answer: The minimum value of k is 6 . akash_kumar 9 answered Feb 27 akash_kumar 9 comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes Prashant-G answered Mar 23 Prashant-G comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. 0 0 votes . Three processes $(P_1, P_2, P_3)$ are given. Two binary semaphores are initialized as $(A=2)$ and $(B=0)$. A shared variable $(x)$ is initialized as $(x=0)$.

Each process executes the following code:

wait(A);
printf("*");
x = x + 1;
if (x == 2) { 
    printf("$"); 
    signal(B);
}
wait(B);
signal(A);
printf("#");
signal(B);

Which of the following outputs is possible?

questions.explanation: Given Processes: P1, P2, P3 Semaphores: A = 2 (counting semaphore) B = 0 Shared variable x = 0 Each process executes: wait(A); printf("*"); x = x + 1; if (x == 2) { printf("$"); signal(B); } wait(B); signal(A); printf("#"); signal(B); Important Observations A = 2 → Only two processes can enter initially . → The third process waits . Each process prints: one "*" one "#" So total output must contain: 3 stars (*) 3 hashes (#) "$" prints only once because it prints when x == 2 . B = 0 initially → All processes block at wait(B) until the process where x = 2 executes signal(B) . Step-by-Step Execution (Typical Case) Step 1 Two processes enter (say P1 and P2 ). P1: wait(A) → print * P2: wait(A) → print * Output: ** Step 2 Update x P1 → x = 1 P2 → x = 2 When x = 2 printf("$") signal(B) Output: **$ Step 3 Now B = 1 , so one process continues past wait(B) . Example order: P2 continues signal(A) print # signal(B) Output **$# Step 4 Second process passes wait(B) P1 continues signal(A) print # sig

questions.questionHtml:
Let $M$ be a randomly chosen non-empty subset of $S=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 2026\}$.

Which of the following is the probability that the product of all the elements of $M$ is even?

  1. $2^{1013}\left(2^{1013}-1\right) / 2^{2026}$
  2. $2^{1013} / 2^{2026}$
  3. $2^{1013}\left(2^{1013}-1\right) /\left(2^{2026}-1\right)$
  4. $1 /\left(2^{2026}-1\right)$
questions.explanation: S = {1,2,3,....,2026} Total number of non-empty subsets of S: \[ 2^{2026} - 1 \] The product of elements of M is even if and only if M contains at least one even number. There are 2026 numbers in S. Number of even numbers = 1013   Number of odd numbers = 1013 The product is not even (i.e., odd) only if all selected elements are odd. Number of subsets formed only from odd numbers: \[ 2^{1013} - 1 \] Hence, number of subsets whose product is even: \[ (2^{2026} - 1) - (2^{1013} - 1) \] \[ = 2^{2026} - 2^{1013} \] \[ = 2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1) \] Therefore, required probability: \[ \frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1} \] Correct option: \[ {(C)} \]

Let

\[

\]

codeBlocks: Hence 0.5 is accurate.
questions.explanation: Special Note: This question is taken from the exercise section of the textbook: A First Course In Probability by Sheldon M. Ross. \[ L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} \] The term \[ \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} \] is the PMF of a Poisson random variable with parameter $\lambda = n$. Hence, \[ \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{e^{-n} n^k}{k!} = P(X \le n), \quad X \sim \text{Poisson}(n). \] For large $n$, we use Central Limit Theorem(CLT) \[ X \sim \text{Poisson}(n) \] has \[ \mathbb{E}[X] = n, \quad \operatorname{Var}(X) = n. \] Thus, \[ X \approx N(n,n). \] Since we are standardizing the random variable $X$ itself, \[ Z = \frac{X - n}{\sqrt{n}}. \] (We divide by the standard deviation $\sqrt{n}$, not by $\sqrt{n}/\sqrt{n}$, because we are not dealing with a sample mean.) Therefore, \[ P(X \le n) = P\left( \frac{X-n}{\sqrt{n}} \le 0 \right). \] As $n \to \infty$, \[ \frac{X-n}{\sqrt{n}} \to N(0,1). \] Hence, \[ P(Z \le 0) = 0.5. \] \[ \boxed{L = 0.5} \] Correct Option: (A)

It is also known that among the general population, the disease $\text{D}$ occurs in $30 \%$ of the individuals.

If a person tests positive for $\text{D}$ in that clinic, the probability that he/she actually suffers from the disease $\text{D}$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation: Let D = person has disease $\bar{D}$ = person does not have disease + = test result is positive   Given: \[ P(D) = 0.30, \quad P(\bar D) = 0.70 \] \[ P(+|D) = 0.80 \] \[ P(+|\bar D) = 0.10 \] We need to compute: \[ P(D|+) \] Using Bayes’ theorem: \[ P(D|+) = \frac{P(+|D)P(D)} {P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|\bar D)P(\bar D)} \] Substituting values: \[ P(D|+) = \frac{0.80 \times 0.30} {0.80 \times 0.30 + 0.10 \times 0.70} \] \[ = \frac{0.24} {0.24 + 0.07} = \frac{0.24}{0.31} \] \[ = 0.77419 \] Rounded to two decimal places: \[ \boxed{0.77} \] Aditya Jyotishi answered Feb 24 • moved Feb 27 by Misbah Ghaya Aditya Jyotishi comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. (Answer in integer )
questions.questionHtml:
For a given data set $\left\{x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right\}$, where $n=100$, it is known that
\[
\frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-x_{j}\right)^{2}=99
\]
Let us denote $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i}$

The value of $\frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Solution: Given: \[ n = 100 \] \[ \frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 99 \] We use the following important identity: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2n \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \] This identity relates the total pairwise squared differences to the total sum of squared deviations from the mean. It follows from expanding \[ (x_i - x_j)^2 = (x_i - \bar{x} - (x_j - \bar{x}))^2 \] and simplifying using \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0. \] Now apply the identity. Since \( n = 100 \), \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (x_i - x_j)^2 = 2(100) \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 200 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \] Substitute into the given equation: \[ \frac{1}{2000} \cdot 200 \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 99 \] \[ \frac{1}{10} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 99 \] \[ \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = 990 \] Now compute the required value: \[ \frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \frac{990}{99} = 10 \] Final Answer: \[ \boxed{10} \] Aditya Jyotishi

questions.explanation: We can choose $ n_i $ for $$ n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + n_4 = 20,\quad n_i \ge 0 $$ in $$ \binom{20 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{23}{3} $$ ways.  Now the requirement is $ n_i \ge 1 $. So write each variable as: $$ n_i = x_i + 1,\quad x_i \ge 0 $$ Substituting: $$ (x_1+1) + (x_2+1) + (x_3+1) + (x_4+1) = 20 $$ $$ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 + 4 = 20 $$ $$ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 16,\quad x_i \ge 0 $$ Number of solutions: $$ \binom{16 + 4 - 1}{4 - 1} = \binom{19}{3} $$ Therefore, $$ P = \frac{\binom{19}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}} $$ Devanshu_Gaur answered Feb 17 Devanshu_Gaur comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $$S=\{1,2,3,\ldots,2026\}$$A non-empty subset $M \subseteq S$ is chosen uniformly at random.

What is the probability that the product of all elements of $M$ is even?

  1. $\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$

     
  2. $\dfrac{2^{1013}}{2^{2026}}$

     
  3. $\dfrac{1}{2^{2026}-1}$

     
  4. $\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}}$
questions.explanation: 1. Probability of an even product Answer: A. $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$ The set $S$ has 2026 elements, 1013 of which are even and 1013 of which are odd. The total number of non-empty subsets of $S$ is $2^{2026} - 1$. The product of elements in a subset $M$ is even if and only if $M$ contains at least one even number. It is easier to calculate the probability of the complementary event: the product is odd. The product is odd if and only if all elements in $M$ are odd. The number of odd elements in $S$ is 1013. The number of non-empty subsets containing only odd elements is $2^{1013} - 1$. The probability that the product is odd is $\frac{2^{1013} - 1}{2^{2026} - 1}$. The probability that the product is even is $1 - \frac{2^{1013} - 1}{2^{2026} - 1} = \frac{(2^{2026} - 1) - (2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1} = \frac{2^{2026} - 2^{1013}}{2^{2026} - 1}$. Factoring out $2^{1013}$ from the numerator gives the final answer: $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1}$. Het_Prajapa

[ 1 ] $E[XY] = 0.3 \times 0 = 0$ To find $\text{Var}((2X-1)Y)$, we will use the formula $\text{Var}(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2$. First, find $E[(2X-1)Y]$: $E[(2X-1)Y] = E[2XY - Y] = 2E[XY] - E[Y]$ $E[(2X-1)Y] = 2 \times 0 - 0 = 0$ Step 3: Calculate E[((2X-1)Y)²] $E[((2X-1)Y)^2] = E[(4X^2 - 4X + 1)Y^2] = E[(4(X^2 - X) + 1)Y^2]$ Since $X$ is a Bernoulli random variable, $X^2 = X$ (as $0^2=0$ and $1^2=1$). So, $X^2 - X = 0$. $E[((2X-1)Y)^2] = E[(4 \times 0 + 1)Y^2] = E[Y^2]$ Use the variance formula $\text{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2$ to find $E[Y^2]$: $E[Y^2] = \text{Var}(Y) + (E[Y])^2 = 100 + 0^2 = 100$

questions.questionHtml:
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with CDF $F(x)$.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. $F(x)$ is always a positive function
     
  2. $F(x)$ has jump discontinuity
     
  3. $F(x)$ is a non-decreasing function
     
  4. $F(x)$ is left continuous
questions.explanation: Answer: (B) F(x) has jump discontinuity and (C) F(x) is a non-decreasing function The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of any random variable, whether discrete or continuous, is always a non-decreasing function. Therefore, statement C is true. For a discrete random variable, the CDF is a step function. It increases in jumps at the points where the random variable has a non-zero probability. These jumps are defined as jump discontinuities. Therefore, statement B is true. Statement A is false because $F(x)$ is defined as a probability and ranges from 0 to 1, so it is non-negative, but not always strictly positive (it is 0 for values below the minimum possible value of the random variable). Statement D is false because the CDF of a discrete random variable is always right-continuous, not left-continuous. questions.questionHtml:
Let $X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. Given that $P(X>5)=0.35$.

Find the value of $P(X>10 \mid X>5)$.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Understand the memoryless property The exponential distribution is memoryless, meaning that the probability of a future event does not depend on past events, given that the past event has already occurred. Mathematically, for $s, t > 0$, the property is expressed as $P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$. Step 2: Apply the property In this problem, we have $s = 5$ and $t = 5$. We want to find $P(X > 10 \mid X > 5)$, which can be written as $P(X > 5+5 \mid X > 5)$. Step 3: Use the given information According to the memoryless property, $P(X > 5+5 \mid X > 5) = P(X > 5)$. We are given that $P(X > 5) = 0.35$. Answer: The value of $P(X > 10 \mid X > 5)$ is $\mathbf{0.35}$. questions.questionHtml:
​​​​​​A recursive function in Python is given.

def mystery(n):
    if n <= 0:
        return 1
    else:
        return mystery(n-1) + mystery(n-2)

Now, consider the following function call:

mystery(4)

Assume that a typical runtime stack is used to manage function calls. Each function call is pushed onto the stack and removed only after it finishes execution.

Which of the following options denotes the total number of function calls (i.e., the total number of stack activations), including the initial call, to compute mystery$(4)?$

  1. $5$
  2. $9$
  3. $15$

questions.explanation: \[ \texttt{mystery(4)}. \]Recursion Expansion Since $n > 0$, each call generates two further calls: \[ m(n) \rightarrow m(n-1) + m(n-2) \] Expanding m(4) fully down to the base cases: \[ \begin{array}{c}\hspace{1.7cm} m(4) \\[6pt] \begin{array}{cc}\ m(3) & m(2) \\[6pt] \begin{array}{cc} m(2) & \hspace{1cm} m(1) \end{array} & \begin{array}{cc} m(1) & \hspace{1cm}m(0) \end{array} \\[12pt] \begin{array}{cccc} \hspace{1px}m(1) & m(0) & m(0) & m(-1) \end{array} \\[12pt] \begin{array}{cccccc}  \hspace{-1cm} m(-1) & m(0)\ \hspace{1.5cm}& m(-1) & m(0) \end{array} \end{array} \end{array} \] Count all nodes: \[ \begin{aligned} m(4) &: 1 \\ m(3) &: 1 \\ m(2) &: 2 \\ m(1) &: 3 \\ m(0) &: 5 \\ m(-1) &: 3 \\ \end{aligned} \] \[ \text{Total calls} = 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 15 \] \[ \boxed{\text{Total number of function calls} = 15} \] \[ \boxed{\text{Correct option: (C)}} \]

questions.explanation: Answer: B The key to this problem is understanding how default arguments are handled in Python. When lst=[] is used as a default argument, the same list object is created only once when the function is defined, not every time the function is called. Subsequent calls to the function without providing a new list will reuse and modify this single, shared list object.  The first call, append_to_lst(1), uses the default list. The list becomes [1], and [1] is printed. The second call, append_to_lst(2), again uses the same default list object. The value 2 is appended to the existing list, making it [1, 2], and [1, 2] is printed. The third call, append_to_lst(3, []), explicitly provides a new , empty list ([]) as an argument. The value 3 is appended to this new list, making it [3], and [3] is printed. The output will therefore be: [1] [1, 2] [3] Het_Prajapati answered Feb 17 Het_Prajapati comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Voting & Accepting an a
